The Henri van Breda story

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we see the crime scene vidoes

Unique Selling Point:
Crime scene footage and pics. Andre van breda to give interview.

Summary:
The story will be a summing up of the case and will ask questions if his appeal to the Supreme court has any chance. Also a personal story of the prosecutor and the lead police man. Also we will hear an emotional interview with the brother and hear from a forensic psychatrist/psycholist - and the show will, be peppered wth snippets from court

Script:


Operator: What are the injuries?
Henri: umm head injuries...
Operator: Are they conscious?
Henri: I don’t think so. My sister is moving but that’s it.

LINK: That was the chilling recording of then 20-year-old Henri van Breda to an emergency call center. His mother father and brother lay dead while his younger sister’s life was hanging by a thread.

And that call came in 2 hours and forty minutes after the murders had taken place.

On the morning of January 27th 2015, emergency services descended onto the high security De Zalze Winelands golf estate in Stellenbosch. This was the gruesome scene that greeted first responders. A bloody axe on the landing…… 55-year-old Theresa van Breda lay dead at the top of the stairs. The bodies of her husband 54-year-old martin and their son 22 year old Rudi were found in another room. Their daughter 16-year-old Marli had severe head injuries but, was still alive.

She was rushed to hospital while Henri van Breda who would say that he and his family were attacked by an axe wielding intruder, was treated for minor injuries.

The brutality of the attack stunned Sgt Marlon Appolis from the Stellenbosch serious and violent crimes unit.

Sgt Appolis: It always goes through your mind; I mean who would do a crime like this. Who would hate this person so much they would kill them in a manner like this.

He was tasked with collecting physical evidence from Marli who clung to life in hospital.

Henri’s uncle Andre van Breda who lives in Pretoria, vividly recalls the phone call he got that morning from his murdered brothers attorney.

Andre: and he asked me if I am alone. I said no I am at the office. He said okay sit down and then he informed me. It was shocking, absolute, I couldn’t believe it.

Nor could State Advocate Susan Galloway when news filtered through to the NPA offices.

Galloway: It was strange that it was in a security estate which is normally very safe an we all discussing the possibilities of how that could have happened.

No 12 Goske street in the De Zalze estate in Stellenbosch became the home of successful businessman Martin Van Breda, who moved back to SA in 2014 from Australia with his wife Theresa and daughter Marli. Henri Joined them later that year from Australia and was followed by Rudi during his university break.

Andre: There was no conflict in the house. It was a lovely family. Absolutely. Martin and Theresa were those father and mother that you can only wish to have.
Devi: They were close knit?
Andre: Very Close, very close.
Devi: What was Henri like as a young man growing up?
Andre: Devi, Henri was this friendly boy. Of all martin’s children, he was the laughing one, the happy one. If you visit them he will be the first one at the car to carry the bags.

Two weeks after the murders a memorial service was held for the slain family members in Pretoria. Already Andre had his doubts about henry’s story.

Andre: Because his injuries was very small. Why killing three people and not four. I mean its common sense.

Andre took his nephew, Henri aside for a heart to heart.

Devi: So what did you say to him?
Andre: I just asked him. I said to him Henri, what happened and he confirmed an intruder an I said to him, all I expect of you is to tell the truth.

LINK: While the country tried to make sense of the murders, the investigation would take 18 months before an arrest was made.
.

Sgt Marlon Appolis became the lead investigator and worked closely with state advocate Susan Galloway. He first had to investigate Hendri’s version events which was detailed in the statement he gave to the Stellenbosch police.

Appolis: He gave us a scenario of what happened and we had to follow it up because he said it was this guy dressed with a balaclava on and during that time we had a lot of house robberies on farms, farm attacks.


It took the police months to exclude this scenario. The focus then shifted to Henri van Breda.

Galloway: So then you turn back to the person who gave you the information in the first place and then you have to get expert opinions on everything that he says to explain why what he says cannot be true if this is what the objective evidence says.

For example, blood spatter analysis was inconsistent with his version. It took months for DNA evidence to be analyzed. 219 blood samples had to be also processed and many expert witnesses consulted. Finally, an arrest warrant was issued and on the 13th of June 2016 Henri van Breda accompanied by his attorney arrived at the Stellenbosch police station.

Appolis: And he handed himself over and then I arrested him and put him in a cells.
Devi: How did he come across?
Appolis: Well he was like he was in court, cool and calm, as if nothing happened.

Hendri Van Breda's defence was paid for by the family’s trust.

Andre: Its important. That is is why there is family, okay? Even if he is guilty, one must see there is a defence. A proper defence. I mean if it is not him, he needs a good defence.

LINK: The trial started in this court on the 24th of April 2017.. In total the state would call 28 witnesses.

Hendri Van Brea pleaded not guilty to three chargers of murder, one of attempted murder, and one of defeating the ends of justice. He testified how he and his family members were attacked.
A chilling moment during the trial was when he was asked to give a demonstration of how he had defended himself.

Devi: How was he as a witness?
Galloway: His evidence in Chief sounded very rehearsed. Cross examination he was very arrogant, sarcastic at times.



The only other eye witness who could shed light on the truth was marli van bread. Despite having recovered from her injures she did not testify because she suffers from retrograde amnesia.

The state was unable to prove motive and based its case entirely on circumstantial and forensic evidence. it argued that there was no breach in security at the estate, there was no forced entry into the home, valuable such as computers watches were not stolen and that most of Henri van Breda’s injuries were self inflicted.

Trial judge Siraj Desai agreed and passed judgment on the 21st of May 2018.
Sound up: Count 1, the murder of Rudi van Breda, the accused is found guilty.

He was found guilty on three murder charges, one of attempted murder, and of defeating the ends of justice. He was given three life sentences.

Andre who had given evidence in court was there when judgment was pronounced.

Andre: Myself and my brother, we accept the ruling of the court and we abide by that.

The defence handed in a 28-page application for leave to appeal against the judgment and sentences. Many reasons were put forward including that dna analysis corroborated that Hendri van Breda was not near his mother and sister when they were attacked and the absence of any of Marli ‘s dna on the axe suggesting that there may have been another attacker armed also with an axe …..but the judge was not swayed.

Sound up: In the result, the application for leave to appeal, both against the convictions and the sentences is refused. Hopefully that’s my last word on this case. The court is adjourned.


The defence is now planning to petition the supreme court of appeal. Associate professor of law and advocate James Grant says that the defence is only able to hand in a 20-page appeal.

Grant: It’s incredibly difficult to persuade them that they may well, on those 20 pages, reach a completely different conclusion to the original judge. So its a high, tis a high threshold.

LINK: While Henri van Breda is behind bars for the murders, one outstanding question has yet to be answered. Why would someone murder his family members in such a brutal way.

It's something that Susan Galloway still ponders upon.
Galloway: My personal view, its a culmination of a festering of a perceived injustice. That the best way I can describe it, but that’s my personal view.
Devi: Over a period of years?
Galloway: Over a period of years. I think for his whole life he has ha this perceived injustice towards him.
Andre: I still want to know why. I still want to know why.

Andre, who has visited Henri in prison spoke about the deep love and respect he and his twin brother had for martin and the family. He still struggles with the thoughts of what they had to endure.

Andre: I don’t want to think what happened in that room. I can’t imagine, I can’t imagine.
